updates.name: Dieffenbachia (dumb cane), lime/cream form
updates.note: About this plant filled in, with sources (batch A5)

growth_habit: Evergreen tropical perennial with a thick cane-like stem (an aroid)
lifespan: Many years; old canes get leggy and can be cut back
zone_notes: Leaves are damaged below about 45 to 50°F, so it is a houseplant and summer patio plant here.
native_range: Tropical Central and South America and the Caribbean, in shady, moist forest.
conservation_status: No IUCN Red List assessment that Claude could confirm. Garden plants are cultivars.
bloom: A small greenish-white spathe and spadix, hidden among the leaves; uncommon indoors.
fruit: Small orange-red berries after flowering, rarely seen indoors. Not edible.
danger_humans: All parts contain needle-like calcium oxalate crystals. Chewing them causes burning pain and swelling of the mouth, tongue and throat, drooling and trouble swallowing; the sap can irritate skin and eyes. Rarely serious, but keep it from children and wash your hands after pruning. Its old name "dumb cane" comes from the mouth swelling, which can stop speech for a while.
danger_animals: Toxic to cats and dogs (ASPCA): the calcium oxalate crystals cause pawing at the mouth, drooling, mouth swelling, vomiting and trouble swallowing.
propagation:
Cane cuttings: cut a bare stem into 2 to 3 in pieces with a node each, lay them half-buried in moist mix, keep warm (70 to 80°F).
Tip cuttings rooted in water or moist mix.
Air layering a tall, leggy cane, then cutting it off once roots show.

updates.name: Fig
updates.note: About this plant filled in, with sources (batch A5)

growth_habit: Deciduous fruit tree or large shrub
zone_notes: Hardy in the ground in Central Texas. Young trees can be frozen to the ground in a hard freeze and regrow from the roots.
native_range: Southwest Asia and the eastern Mediterranean; grown for thousands of years.
conservation_status: No IUCN Red List assessment that Claude could confirm.
bloom: No visible flowers: the tiny flowers are inside the developing fig.
fruit: Edible figs, usually summer and sometimes again in fall. Common figs in Texas set fruit without pollination.
danger_humans: The milky sap irritates skin and, with sunlight, can cause blistering burns (phytophotodermatitis). Wear gloves and long sleeves when pruning.
danger_animals: The leaves and sap are toxic to cats and dogs (ASPCA): vomiting, drooling and skin irritation. Ripe fruit in small amounts is not a known danger.
propagation:
Hardwood cuttings in late winter, pencil-thick and 8 to 10 in long, set mostly into the soil.
Softwood cuttings in early summer.
Air layering or ground layering a low branch.

updates.name: Grape vine (young)
updates.note: About this plant filled in, with sources (batch A5)

growth_habit: Deciduous woody vine climbing with tendrils
height_ground: Climbs 40 ft or more into trees
height_pot: Needs a trellis; 6 to 10 ft in a big container
zone_notes: A native of Central Texas, fully hardy here.
native_range: Texas and nearby states (Oklahoma, Louisiana, Arkansas, Alabama); common in Central Texas along creeks and fencerows.
conservation_status: No IUCN Red List assessment that Claude could confirm. Common in its range.
invasive: Native here, but it can smother trees and shrubs if left unchecked.

danger_animals: Grapes and raisins can cause sudden kidney failure in dogs, and possibly cats, even in small amounts. Keep dogs away from fallen fruit.

Hardwood cuttings in winter.
Layering a long cane into the soil.
Seed, though many seedlings are male and fruitless.

updates.name: Prickly pear (opuntia)
updates.note: About this plant filled in, with sources (batch A5)

growth_habit: Cactus with flat jointed pads
zone_notes: Opuntia ficus-indica is damaged in hard freezes below about 15 to 20°F. Native Texas prickly pears (Opuntia engelmannii) are hardier.
native_range: Opuntia ficus-indica is from Mexico, domesticated there long ago and now grown worldwide. The genus is native from Canada to Argentina, including Texas.
conservation_status: All cacti are on CITES Appendix II, which controls international trade. No IUCN Red List assessment that Claude could confirm.
invasive: Opuntia ficus-indica is a serious invasive in Australia and South Africa; not a concern in Texas, where prickly pears are native.
bloom: Large yellow to orange cup flowers in spring.
fruit: Edible fruit ("tunas"), and young pads ("nopales") are eaten as a vegetable once the spines and glochids are removed.
danger_humans: Not poisonous, but besides the large spines it has glochids: tiny barbed hairs that come off in clusters and are hard to remove from skin. Use tongs and thick gloves; tape lifts glochids.
danger_animals: Not poisonous; the danger is spines in mouths, paws and fur.
propagation:
Pad cuttings: cut a pad at the joint, let it callus for a week, and set it upright in dry gritty soil.
Seed.

growth_habit: Small clumping succulent rosette (a dwarf aloe hybrid)
zone_notes: Damaged below about 28 to 32°F.
native_range: A cultivated hybrid, with no wild range. Its parents are dwarf aloes from Madagascar and southern Africa.
conservation_status: Not applicable: a cultivated hybrid.
bloom: Thin spikes of orange to coral tube flowers.
danger_humans: Not known to be seriously poisonous; do not eat it.
danger_animals: Aloes are listed as toxic to cats and dogs (ASPCA): vomiting and diarrhea if chewed.
propagation: Separate pups with roots.

updates.name: Philodendron 'Ring of Fire'
updates.note: About this plant filled in, with sources (batch A5)

growth_habit: Evergreen tropical aroid, a self-heading or slowly climbing hybrid
height_ground: Not grown in the ground here; 2 to 4 ft where it is
zone_notes: Damaged below about 50°F; a houseplant here.
native_range: A cultivated hybrid or mutation, with no wild range. Its parents are Philodendron species from tropical Central and South America.
conservation_status: Not applicable: a cultivated hybrid.
bloom: Rare indoors.
danger_humans: All parts contain needle-like calcium oxalate crystals. Chewing them causes burning pain and swelling of the mouth, tongue and throat, drooling and trouble swallowing; the sap can irritate skin and eyes. Rarely serious, but keep it from children and wash your hands after pruning.
danger_animals: Toxic to cats and dogs (ASPCA): the calcium oxalate crystals cause pawing at the mouth, drooling, mouth swelling, vomiting and trouble swallowing.
propagation:
Stem or node cuttings rooted in water, moss or moist chunky mix.
Separate offshoots (pups) with their own roots from the base.
Many of these hybrids can revert or change pattern when grown from cuttings; tissue-cultured plants keep the look best.
